concept.body:
Three questions decide whether an input may go into an AI tool: **Which data class?** **Is exactly this combination of tool, purpose and data class approved?** **Does the purpose need the detail at all?** The third question is data minimisation, a GDPR principle (Art. 5(1)(c)).

An example model with four levels that your organization adapts:

| Level | Example | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Public | approved website text | check rights and currency |
| Internal | project plan, minutes | approved tools only |
| Confidential | customer list, supplier terms | approval plus contract, configuration, permissions |
| Specially protected | salary, health, applications | general assistants blocked |

Passwords and other credentials never go into a prompt, at any level.
concept.takeaway: Classify before you type: level, approval, minimisation. If one answer is missing, enter nothing.

exercise.title: Sort twelve data snippets
exercise.instructions: Put each card on the matching pile. After each card you see straight away why it belongs there. The levels are assumptions for a fictional company.

items.text: Press release that has been on the website since Monday
items.why: Already published. Still check that you use the current version and hold the rights.

items.text: Product catalogue PDF from the website
items.why: Publicly available. Version and approved use still need checking.
Not for outsiders, but no special protection need. Only in an approved tool, names only if the purpose needs them.
Typically internal: belongs in a workflow approved for internal data.

items.text: Customer list with names and e-mail addresses
items.why: Personal data: purpose, legal basis, processing agreement and minimisation must fit.
Usually confidential by contract. Only with approval for confidential data and matching permissions.
Unpublished figure: confidentiality and access rules apply until it is published.
Serious harm if mishandled. Only in specialist systems approved for it, never in general assistants.
Health data is a special category under GDPR Art. 9 and needs special protection.
Decisions about people, many personal details: only in the approved hiring process.

items.text: API key for the shop system
items.why: Credentials open systems. They never go into a prompt, at any level.
Like any credential: never enter it. If you suspect a leak, change it and report it.

checks.prompt: A colleague wants to upload a customer list to an AI tool. The tool has an enterprise licence. What decides whether she may?

options.feedback: A licence says nothing about whether exactly this purpose with this data class is approved.

options.text: Whether tool, purpose and data class are approved together and whether the purpose needs every detail.
Whether training use is switched off.
options.feedback: The switch replaces neither contract nor legal basis nor permissions.

checks.explanation: Approvals apply to combinations of tool, purpose and data class. Add data minimisation: what the purpose does not need stays out.

checks.prompt: You cannot find out whether a tool is approved for confidential data. What do you do?

options.text: Enter it carefully and delete the history afterwards.
options.feedback: The data is transferred the moment you enter it. Deleting afterwards does not undo that.

options.text: Enter nothing and ask your organization's approval route.
Translate the data into another language, then enter it.
options.feedback: A translation does not change the data class.

checks.explanation: If one answer on level, approval or minimisation is missing, you enter nothing. Asking is faster than an incident.

concept.body:
Ask about every detail: **Does the task need this?** To reply to a complaint, a model needs the facts of the case, not the IBAN, mobile number or home address. Leaving details out or replacing them with placeholders is data minimisation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c)).

Two limits:

- **Redaction does not make an unapproved tool acceptable.** It lowers the risk inside an approved workflow.
- **Pseudonymised data stays personal data** as long as the person can be identified again with additional information (GDPR Art. 4(5), Recital 26).

Pattern matching finds e-mail addresses, phone numbers and IBANs. No pattern reliably finds names in running text, health details or trade secrets: you check those yourself.
concept.takeaway: Redact everything the purpose does not need. It does not replace an approval.

exercise.title: Make the complaint ready to paste
exercise.instructions: You want to draft a reply with the approved company assistant. Tap every detail the draft does not need, then check the result. All data is made up.

segments.pii: Name: "the customer" is enough for the draft.

segments.text: from Bergmann Hydraulik. Our order of

segments.pii: IBAN: payments go through accounting, never through a draft.
Private mobile number: not needed for the text.
E-mail address: the reply goes to the sender anyway.

segments.text: . I expect an explanation of how future delays will be prevented.

checks.prompt: You redacted every name and number. May you now paste the text into a private, unapproved chat service?

options.text: Yes, once redacted the text may go into any tool.
options.feedback: Context, business details and inferences remain, and the tool has not been checked.

options.text: No. Redaction lowers the risk but does not replace approval of the tool.
Yes, if you delete the history afterwards.
options.feedback: The transfer happened when you entered it.

checks.explanation: Redaction is one step inside an approved workflow, not a pass for any service.

checks.prompt: You replace "Petra Sommerfeld" with "Customer K-17" and keep a mapping list. How does the GDPR treat the data?

options.text: As anonymous, so no data protection rules apply.
options.feedback: They would only be anonymous if nobody could identify the person again with reasonable effort.

options.text: As pseudonymised, and therefore still personal data.
As public, because no name remains.
options.feedback: Public is a data class for published material, not a result of redaction.

checks.explanation: With the mapping list the person can be identified again. Such data is pseudonymised and stays personal data (GDPR Art. 4(5), Recital 26).
